# Born in the Nest: full text

> Gentle, US-focused education about birth choices (home birth, birth centers, hospitals), fear of childbirth and first-time mom choices. Education only, not medical advice. Source: https://borninthenest.com

## Home birth & birth center FAQ · Born in the Nest
URL: https://borninthenest.com/faq.html
Gentle, sourced answers: is home birth safe, home birth vs birth center, finding a midwife, home birth cost, fear of childbirth and first-time mom choices.

FAQ
Gentle answers to your birth questions
Home birth, birth centers, midwives and fear of birth, answered gently and honestly.

These are the questions I hear most, and the ones I wish I'd asked before my first birth. Each answer is short, honest and linked to its sources, so you can read more and take it to your midwife or doctor.

What are my options for where to give birth in the US?
You can plan to give birth at home with a qualified midwife, in a freestanding birth center, or in a hospital. ACOG, the professional organization of US obstetricians, says clearly that you have the right to choose where you give birth, and encourages you to learn the benefits and risks of each option first.

Most US babies are born in hospitals. In 2024, about 1.6% were born at home and about 0.6% in birth centers, so if you've never heard much about the other two options, you're not alone.

Sources ACOG, Planned Home Birth FAQ · CDC/NCHS final birth data for 2024 (Natality User Guide, Tables 14–15)

What are the alternatives to a hospital birth?
The two main alternatives are a planned home birth and a birth center birth. Both are usually led by midwives, built around undisturbed, low-intervention birth, and planned with a clear path to a hospital if more help is needed.

A birth center is a freestanding, home-like place for birth. The American Association of Birth Centers describes it as "a maximized home rather than a mini-hospital." If a hospital is the right place for you, many hospitals also offer midwife care and low-intervention options.

Sources American Association of Birth Centers, What is a birth center? · ACOG, Planned Home Birth FAQ

Is home birth safe?
It's a question every mom should ask, and I'm so glad you're asking it. The honest answer depends on your own health and your own pregnancy, so it's different for every one of us. An experienced midwife will look at your whole picture with you and tell you honestly whether home birth is a good fit for you. For me, with my midwives, I felt safe, cared for and loved.

Is home birth safe for a first baby?
Every pregnancy is different, and with a first baby there's so much that's new. The kindest next step is to talk it through with an experienced midwife and your care provider, who can look at your health and your pregnancy with you. Many first-time moms also love the idea of a birth center (a midwife-led unit), a calm, home-like middle path.

A first labor often takes its time, so plans can change along the way, and that's okay. That's one reason a birth center can be a beautiful choice for a first baby. Many first-time moms do plan a home birth, and your midwife can help you weigh it for your own pregnancy.

Home birth vs birth center: what's the difference?
With a home birth, your midwife comes to you. You labor in your own space, in your own bed or a birth pool, with only the people you choose. With a birth center, you go to a home-like place run by midwives, often with large beds and birth tubs, and with arrangements for transfer to a hospital when needed.

Both are midwife-led and built for healthy, low-risk pregnancies. In a large US study of birth centers, 84 in 100 women gave birth at the center and 6 in 100 had a cesarean. Choosing between them often comes down to where you feel most relaxed, how far you live from a hospital, and what's available near you.

Sources American Association of Birth Centers · Stapleton et al. 2013, National Birth Center Study II

Who is a good candidate for a home birth or birth center?
Out-of-hospital birth is planned for healthy, low-risk pregnancies. According to ACOG, it's generally considered when you're carrying one baby, the baby is head-down, you're between about 37 and 42 weeks, and you don't have conditions like diabetes, high blood pressure or preeclampsia. ACOG recommends against planned home birth for a baby who isn't head-down, for twins, and after a previous cesarean.

If you've had a cesarean before, talk this through carefully with your provider, because guidelines and state rules differ. Your midwife will keep checking throughout pregnancy and labor, and plans can change gently if your needs change.

Sources ACOG, Planned Home Birth FAQ

What happens if I need to go to the hospital during labor?
In a US study of nearly 17,000 planned home births, about 9 out of 10 women gave birth at home. When plans changed, it was usually because of a long, slow labor. If this is your first baby, it's worth talking through your plan early with your midwife.

Your midwife comes with you and shares your notes. A good midwife talks about her transfer plan at your very first visit: which hospital, how long it takes to get there, and when she'd recommend going.

Sources Cheyney et al. 2014, MANA Statistics Project

How do I find a midwife?
Start with the directories: the ACNM Find a Midwife search for certified nurse-midwives, NARM to verify a certified professional midwife, and the American Association of Birth Centers to find a birth center near you. Then book a free consultation with one or two midwives. Most offer one.

Ask about her training and experience, who her backup is, her transfer plan and hospital, what equipment and medicines she brings, and what it costs. Then notice how you feel after talking with her. Calm and heard is a very good sign.

Sources ACNM · NARM · AABC

What's the difference between a CNM, a CM and a CPM?
A certified nurse-midwife (CNM) is a registered nurse with graduate midwifery education. CNMs are licensed in all 50 states and DC, and they work in hospitals, birth centers and homes. A certified midwife (CM) has the same midwifery education without the nursing degree, and is licensed in fewer states. A certified professional midwife (CPM) is certified by NARM and specializes in birth at home and in birth centers. CPMs are licensed in 37 states and DC.

Which one you choose often depends on where you want to give birth and what your state allows. Insurance coverage also differs, so it's worth asking each midwife.

Sources ACNM comparison of CNM, CM and CPM credentials (2026)

How much does a home birth cost?
A 2021 nationwide study estimated the average fee for a US home birth at about $4,650, ranging from $2,000 to about $9,900. That usually covers prenatal visits, the birth and postpartum care. The same study cited estimates of about $8,300 for a birth center birth and about $13,600 for a vaginal hospital birth, before insurance.

What you actually pay depends on your insurance and your state. Many midwives will help you check your coverage, so it's a great question for your first consultation.

Sources Anderson & Gilkison 2021, The Cost of Home Birth in the United States

I'm scared of giving birth. Is that normal?
Yes, it's very normal, and you're not alone. Most of us feel some worry about birth. Research suggests that about 14 in 100 pregnant women worldwide feel a severe fear of childbirth, and about 16 in 100 first-time moms. So much of what we've seen of birth comes from movies, where it's always an emergency.

What helps: learning how birth really works, knowing your options, a midwife or doctor you trust who gets to know you, and practicing calm breathing and relaxation. If your fear feels too big, please tell your provider. You can also call or text the free, confidential National Maternal Mental Health Hotline at 1-833-TLC-MAMA (1-833-852-6262), 24/7.

Sources O'Connell et al. 2017, Acta Obstet Gynecol Scand · National Maternal Mental Health Hotline (HRSA)

What is tokophobia?
Tokophobia is a severe fear of pregnancy and childbirth, strong enough to affect daily life or decisions about pregnancy. It can happen before a first birth (sometimes called primary tokophobia) or after a difficult previous birth (secondary tokophobia). It's real, it's common, and it's treatable.

If this sounds like you, please talk to your midwife or doctor. They can connect you with counseling and help you make a birth plan that feels safe. You deserve support, not judgment.

Sources NHS United Lincolnshire Hospitals, Fear of childbirth · O'Connell et al. 2017

Does having a midwife I know really make a difference?
It can. A Cochrane review of 15 trials with more than 17,000 women compared midwife-led continuity of care, where you get to know your midwife, with other models of care. Women in midwife-led continuity care were less likely to have an epidural or an instrumental birth, more likely to have a spontaneous vaginal birth, and most studies found they were more satisfied with their care.

Sources Sandall et al. 2016, Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews

Can a birth pool or warm water help with pain?
Warm water is one of the gentlest comfort tools. A Cochrane review found that being in water during the first stage of labor may lower the need for an epidural (about 39 in 100 women compared with 43 in 100). Many women also simply find it calming. Ask your midwife or birth center about birth pools and tubs.

Sources Cluett et al. 2018, Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews

What is hypnobirthing?
Hypnobirthing is a childbirth education approach that uses deep relaxation, slow breathing and visualization to help you stay calm in labor. It's built on the idea of the fear-tension-pain cycle, first described by Grantly Dick-Read: fear makes the body tense, and tension makes pain feel stronger. The best-known method is HypnoBirthing: The Mongan Method by Marie Mongan.

Sources OpenStax Maternal-Newborn Nursing, 14.3 Hypnobirthing: The Mongan Method

Is Born in the Nest medical advice?
No. Born in the Nest shares education and encouragement from one mom to another. It doesn't replace care from your licensed midwife or doctor, so please talk to your provider about anything health-related. In an emergency, call 911.

## Your birth options in the US: home, birth center or hospital
URL: https://borninthenest.com/guides/birth-options-home-birth-center-hospital.html
A gentle, honest guide to where you can give birth in the US: home birth with a midwife, a birth center, or a hospital, and how to choose what feels right.

Gentle guide
🏡Your birth options in the US: home, birth center or hospital
Three places, three kinds of care, and one gentle question to help you choose.

Before my first birth, no one ever asked me where I wanted to give birth. I didn't even know it was a choice. Here's what I wish someone had told me: in the US you can plan to give birth at home, in a birth center or in a hospital, and you have the right to choose.

🏡 Home birth

At a planned home birth, a midwife cares for you through pregnancy, comes to you when labor begins, and stays with you through the birth and the first hours after. Prenatal visits are often long and unhurried, sometimes in your own living room. In labor you can move, eat, rest, use a birth pool and be surrounded only by the people you choose.

Midwives bring equipment to listen to your baby, check your blood pressure, help with bleeding and help a baby breathe if needed, and they plan a route to a hospital from the very first visit. For healthy, low-risk pregnancies, large studies have found fewer interventions at home, such as inductions, episiotomies and cesareans. If this is your first baby, remember that every pregnancy is different. Talk it through with an experienced midwife and your care provider, so you can choose what feels right for you.

🌿 Birth center

A birth center is a freestanding, home-like place run by midwives. The American Association of Birth Centers calls it "a maximized home rather than a mini-hospital," with comfy beds, birth tubs and family welcome, plus arrangements for transfer to a hospital when needed.

It's a beautiful middle path, and a lovely choice for a first baby. In a large US study of 79 birth centers, 84 in 100 women gave birth at the center and 6 in 100 had a cesarean.

🏥 Hospital

A hospital is the right place for higher-risk pregnancies, for twins or a baby who isn't head-down, and if you know you'd like an epidural. I'm grateful hospitals exist for when something needs more help. Many hospitals offer midwife care too, and you can still bring calm with you: dim lights, your own music, your breathing and the people you love.

How to choose, gently

Close your eyes for a moment and ask yourself: where would I feel safest, calmest and most loved? Your body does its best work where you can relax. Then bring that answer to the practical questions:

Is my pregnancy healthy and low-risk? Your provider can tell you, and it can change, so keep asking.
How far is the nearest hospital, and what is the midwife's transfer plan?
Which midwives and birth centers are near me, and what does my insurance cover?
Who do I want in the room with me?

Your first steps

Find a midwife or birth center. Try the ACNM Find a Midwife search, NARM for certified professional midwives, and the AABC birth center directory.
Book a free consultation with one or two. Most offer one.
Ask your questions about training, backup, transfer plan, equipment and cost.
Notice how you feel afterward. Calm and heard is a very good sign.

Want more answers? Read the gentle FAQ, or start with my five free lessons.

Sources ACOG, Planned Home Birth FAQ · AABC · Stapleton et al. 2013

With love from my nest to yours,Sybille 🤍

## Scared of giving birth? You are not alone · Born in the Nest
URL: https://borninthenest.com/guides/scared-of-giving-birth.html
Afraid of giving birth? You're not alone. Where fear of childbirth comes from, why calm matters to your body, and gentle things that really help.

Gentle guide
🤍Scared of giving birth? You are not alone
Fear of birth is so common. Here's where it comes from, and what gently helps.

If you're scared of giving birth, I want you to hear this first: there is nothing wrong with you. Most of us feel some worry about birth, and many women feel real fear. Research suggests that about 14 in 100 pregnant women worldwide have a severe fear of childbirth, and about 16 in 100 first-time moms. You are in very good company.

Where the fear comes from

In the movies, birth is a woman screaming while everyone rushes around her. We've seen that scene so many times that most of us grow up believing it's what birth is. Add a few scary stories from friends, and it makes sense that fear moves in long before labor does.

But birth doesn't have to look like that. Yes, there's intensity, and there can be pain. But pain and suffering aren't the same thing.

Why feeling calm matters to your body

Labor is guided by hormones. Oxytocin, often called the love hormone, powers contractions, and endorphins are your body's own comfort. They flow best when you feel safe, private and undisturbed. When you feel afraid or rushed, stress hormones like adrenaline rise, and they can slow labor down.

Childbirth pioneer Grantly Dick-Read called this the fear-tension-pain cycle: fear makes us tense, and tension makes pain feel stronger. The good news is that the cycle works the other way too. Feeling safe and supported helps your body soften and open.

Gentle things that help

Learning how birth really works. The unknown is scary. Knowing what labor actually looks like takes away a lot of fear.
Knowing your options. You can choose where you give birth and who is with you. Read about your birth options.
A midwife or doctor who knows you. In a Cochrane review, women who had continuity of care with a known midwife were less likely to need an epidural, and most studies found they felt more satisfied with their care.
Practicing calm breathing. Slow breaths, longer on the out-breath, practiced for weeks before so your body knows them.
Warm water. A bath or birth pool in labor may lower the need for an epidural.
Your people. Surround yourself with those who make you feel loved. As my midwife Sarah always said, pregnant women need to feel loved.

Confidence can grow, little by little

I didn't feel confident at the start either. My confidence grew month by month, through regular visits with my midwives (monthly at first, then weekly near the end), books and hypnobirthing practice. By month eight, I trusted my body more than I ever had.

When the fear feels too big

Sometimes fear is so strong that it keeps you up at night or changes how you feel about your pregnancy. This is sometimes called tokophobia, and it's real, common and treatable. Please tell your midwife or doctor. They can connect you with counseling and help you make a birth plan that feels safe.

You can also call or text the free, confidential National Maternal Mental Health Hotline at 1-833-TLC-MAMA (1-833-852-6262), any time, day or night. If you're in crisis, call or text 988. In an emergency, call 911.

You deserve to feel supported, not judged. If you'd like a gentle companion along the way, my five free lessons are a lovely place to start.

Sources O'Connell et al. 2017 · Buckley 2015, Hormonal Physiology of Childbearing · Sandall et al. 2016, Cochrane · Cluett et al. 2018, Cochrane · OpenStax, Hypnobirthing · National Maternal Mental Health Hotline

With love from my nest to yours,Sybille 🤍

## First-time mom? What no one tells you about birth choices
URL: https://borninthenest.com/guides/first-time-mom-birth-choices.html
Pregnant with your first baby? The birth choices no one mentions: where to give birth, switching providers, midwives, birth centers and what to ask.

Gentle guide
🌱First-time mom? What no one tells you about your birth choices
The things I wish I'd known before my first baby.

My first baby was born in a hospital, the way most of us are told it should go. No one ever asked me the most important question: where do you want to give birth? I didn't even know it was a choice. No one told me I had other options until my second pregnancy. I want you to know sooner.

1. You get to choose where you give birth

In the US you can plan a birth at home with a midwife, in a birth center or in a hospital. ACOG, the professional organization of US obstetricians, says clearly that you have the right to choose, after learning the benefits and risks of each. Read the gentle overview of your birth options.

2. Midwives aren't only for home births

Certified nurse-midwives are licensed in all 50 states and DC, and they work in hospitals and birth centers as well as homes. Certified professional midwives specialize in birth at home and in birth centers, and they're licensed in 37 states and DC. Many families never meet a midwife simply because no one suggested it.

3. A birth center can be a beautiful choice for a first baby

A birth center is a home-like, midwife-led space with comfy beds and birth tubs, and for many first-time moms it feels like a calm middle path between home and hospital. Every pregnancy is different, so talk your choices through with an experienced midwife and your care provider. I think of birth centers as the great second option.

4. First labors are often longer, and that's okay

A first labor often takes its time. Sometimes a long, slow labor is the reason plans change and you move from home or a birth center to the hospital. Knowing this ahead of time helps you plan calmly instead of feeling like something went wrong.

5. You can ask questions, and you can switch

It's your pregnancy and your birth. You can interview midwives and doctors, ask about their approach, and change providers if something doesn't feel right. Questions I'd ask:

How many births have you attended, and what's your training?
Who is your backup, and who comes with you to births?
What's your transfer plan, and which hospital do you use?
How long are prenatal visits, and how often will we meet?
What does it cost, and will you help me check my insurance?

6. Your feelings matter to your body

Feeling safe, calm and loved isn't a luxury in labor. It helps the hormones of birth do their work. So the question of where to give birth isn't only a medical one. It's also a question of where your body can relax enough to do what it was made to do.

7. You don't have to figure it out alone

Born in the Nest has five free lessons you can read right here, and a weekly letter every Sunday, matched to your due month, all the way to the day you meet your baby. You can also read the FAQ for quick answers.

Sources ACOG, Planned Home Birth FAQ · ACNM credential comparison (2026) · Buckley 2015

With love from my nest to yours,Sybille 🤍

## Why every mammal looks for a nest before giving birth
URL: https://borninthenest.com/lessons/day-1.html
Free lesson 1 of 5 from Born in the Nest: Your body already knows how to do this. Here's what helps it.

Free lesson 1 of 5 · Home birth, explained by a mom who's done it
🪺Why every mammal looks for a nest before giving birth
Your body already knows how to do this. Here's what helps it.

Home birth, explained by a mom who's done it. That's what these five free lessons are, right here on the site, no signup needed.

In the movies, birth is a woman screaming in pain while everyone rushes around her. Most of us have watched that scene a hundred times, and somewhere along the way we started believing it.

But what if birth doesn't have to be like that? Yes, there's intensity, and there can be pain. But pain and suffering aren't the same thing. Birth can be one of the most beautiful, powerful things you'll ever do. We've just been taught to see it through the wrong lens.

I'm Sybille, a mom of two. My first baby was born in a hospital with an epidural. I was completely numb, and I felt helpless. My second was born at home, in my own bed, with a midwife I trusted, and that birth showed me how calm and beautiful giving birth can be. Same body, completely different birth. The biggest difference was where I was and how calm and loved I felt.

As my midwife Sarah always said, pregnant women need to feel loved. That's what Born in the Nest is about.

Hospitals do beautiful, important work, and for some pregnancies they're exactly the right place. And for many of us, birth is also something our bodies were made to do.

So let's start with one question.

Close your eyes for a moment. Where would you feel calmest, most at ease, and most loved?

For many of us, the honest answer is somewhere familiar and quiet, with people we love. And that matters more than we're usually told.

Every mammal looks for a nest. A cat finds a quiet closet. A deer slips into tall grass. When an animal in labor feels watched or threatened, labor often pauses until she's somewhere safe again. Women have been giving birth for as long as there have been people, and we carry that same wisdom.

Here's the gentle science. Labor is guided by hormones, as researcher Dr. Sarah Buckley explains in a detailed review. Oxytocin, the "love hormone," powers contractions. Endorphins are your body's own comfort. When you feel safe, private, and undisturbed, these flow freely. When you feel afraid, rushed, or watched, stress hormones like adrenaline rise, and they can slow labor down. Midwife Ina May Gaskin calls this the Sphincter Law: the body opens best in privacy and calm, the same way none of us can relax in a bathroom with the door wide open. She even found that a relaxed jaw, soft breathing, and laughter help the body open.

Your heart and your womb are connected. Dr. Amali Lokugamage, an obstetrician who planned her own baby's birth at home, explores this in her book The Heart in the Womb. Oxytocin, the hormone that powers labor, is also the hormone of love, trust, and bonding. So when your heart feels safe and loved, your body can soften and open. When you're tense and scared, it tends to hold on. That's not weakness. It's your body protecting you and your baby.

So when you think about where to give birth, it's not only a medical question. It's also a question of where your body can relax enough to do what it was made to do.

A tiny practice for today: take three slow breaths, longer on the out-breath than the in-breath, and notice your shoulders drop. That softening is what we're making room for.

All five lessons

Five short lessons in all. No pressure, no judgment, just what I wish someone had told me before my first birth.

Day 1Why every mammal looks for a nest before giving birth›Day 2What birth looks like when no one's in a hurry›Day 3My two births, and what changed›Day 4My midwives saw what I needed before I said a word›Day 5The question no one asked me before my first birth›

And this isn't a one-time thing. If you'd like, I'll also send you one short, loving letter every Sunday, matched to your due month: one honest moment, one calm idea and one small step for wherever you are. I'll also help with the practical side: how to find and choose a midwife or birth center, and the questions I had when I first decided to switch, answered one by one. These are big decisions, and I wish I'd had someone I could count on when I made them. When I was pregnant, just a message from one of my midwives could calm me down and make my whole day feel lighter. That's what I want Born in the Nest to be for you: a warm, trusted place you can come back to whenever you need it, every week, all the way to the day you meet your baby.

Sources Buckley 2015, Hormonal Physiology of Childbearing · Teaching Normal Birth, Normally (J Perinat Educ), on Ina May Gaskin's work · Amali Lokugamage, The Heart in the Womb (2011)

With love from my nest to yours,Sybille 🤍

## What birth looks like when no one's in a hurry
URL: https://borninthenest.com/lessons/day-2.html
Free lesson 2 of 5 from Born in the Nest: Dim lights, warm water, a midwife who knows your name.

Free lesson 2 of 5 · Home birth, explained by a mom who's done it
🌿What birth looks like when no one's in a hurry
Dim lights, warm water, a midwife who knows your name.

When most of us picture birth, we picture TV: a woman on her back, someone shouting "push!", alarms beeping. It makes sense if that picture feels a little intense. But it's only one picture.

A planned home birth usually looks very different. Here's a gentle peek.

Months before: you'll have regular prenatal visits with your midwife, often an hour long, sometimes in your own living room. You'll talk about nutrition, how you're feeling, your fears, and your hopes. She checks your blood pressure, measures your belly, and listens to your baby's heartbeat. By the time labor starts, she isn't a stranger. She's someone you trust.

When labor begins: you stay home, in your own clothes, eating and drinking when you want, walking around, resting in your bed. You call your midwife, and she comes when it's time.

Fuel for the marathon. At home, you eat and drink whenever you like. Snacks, tea, honey sticks, whatever your body asks for. Labor is a marathon, and you get to fuel it. 🍯 Wherever you give birth, ask ahead what you'll be allowed to eat and drink during labor.

(Personal note: I had a steak dinner, and about five minutes later it was go time. Zero regrets. 🥩)

Who's there: usually your midwife plus a second trained midwife or assistant, your partner, and anyone else you choose: a doula, your mom, a friend. Or no one else at all. At home, you get to choose who shares this moment with you: your partner, your midwives, a dear friend or your mom, and even your older children if they'd like to be there.

(When my second child was born, my first child was there for the first part, just two years old and so proud to help her mama, until it was time for her to go to bed. 💛)

What she brings: midwives come prepared. A typical kit includes a handheld device to listen to baby's heartbeat, a blood pressure cuff, oxygen, equipment to help a baby breathe if needed, medicine to help with bleeding, and supplies for you and your newborn. (What's included depends on her training and your state's rules, so it's a great thing to ask her.)

What it feels like: usually quiet. Soft lights, maybe music, maybe a birth pool. Your midwife watches closely but calmly, often from the corner of the room, checking in without interrupting. Many women say what they remember most is feeling protected.

After the birth: your baby goes straight onto your chest. No one whisks her away. Your midwife checks both of you, helps with the first feed, tidies up, and tucks you into your own bed. She'll come back for check-ups in the days that follow.

Why home can feel so different

This part surprised me most, and I wish someone had told me before my first birth.

A hospital is built to care for many people at once, with kind, hardworking teams who often work in shifts, so the person who greets you may not be the one who catches your baby. That's simply how a big, busy place works, and it's wonderful that it's there.

And here's the beautiful thing: labor isn't a checklist. When labor really gets going, your thinking brain quiets down. Many women describe going inward, almost into another world. You stop following instructions and start following your body. That's exactly what's supposed to happen. It's easier when the lights are soft and the faces are familiar. And if you'd like to do something differently, like wait, move, or say no to something, it helps to know you can always ask for that, and to have people around you who protect your choices.

At home or in a birth center, the care is built around one family: yours. Your midwife has known you for months. She watches closely, but she lets labor unfold at its own pace. And the only people in the room are the ones you choose, the ones who love and support you: your partner, your mom, a dear friend, maybe even your older children.

Your body was made for this. Women have given birth for thousands of years, but many of us have lost touch with that knowing, so we have to learn to tune in again. A good midwife can help you find your way back, and you can practice it yourself. And your baby takes part too. With my second birth, I felt like my baby was guiding me the whole way and taught me so much. For healthy, low-risk pregnancies, a planned home birth with a qualified midwife and a clear backup plan is a real option worth exploring with your provider.

And if plans change? A good midwife has a transfer plan from the very first visit: which hospital, how long it takes, and when she'd recommend going. We'll talk about that on Day 4, because feeling safe also means knowing there's a backup.

A question for you: what part of this picture made you exhale? Write to me at hello@borninthenest.com. I read every message.

Sources ACOG, Planned Home Birth FAQ

With love,Sybille 🤍

## My two births, and what changed · Born in the Nest
URL: https://borninthenest.com/lessons/day-3.html
Free lesson 3 of 5 from Born in the Nest: One in a hospital, one at home. Here's what I learned.

Free lesson 3 of 5 · Home birth, explained by a mom who's done it
💛My two births, and what changed
One in a hospital, one at home. Here's what I learned.

Today I want to share something personal: my two births. Every birth is different, and mine isn't a rulebook. But stories have a way of making things feel possible.

My first baby: the hospital

I was so excited to meet my first baby, and so scared to give birth. Fear guided my whole pregnancy, so I did what was recommended to me without asking many questions. I didn't know there was another way.

I felt uneasy at every hospital check-up, and I wish I'd listened to that feeling sooner. I was induced early. My body wasn't ready, and labor was long, with lots of medication. When it was finally time to push, I had to hold her back until the doctor arrived at 2:30 am.

It felt clinical, and not at all like the birth I'd hoped for. Then the drugs finally wore off, and I was overjoyed with love and the beauty of my baby girl.

My first child is the reason I made different choices for her sister, and why I'm writing this to you.

My second baby: at home

The morning my second child was born felt completely ordinary: coffee, my weekly 45-minute walk, lunch, my daily stretches. When a little cramping started, I barely noticed. I was sure this baby would take at least two more weeks.

In the afternoon I suddenly wanted a bath, after nine months of zero interest. (My midwives laughed later: that's their number one sign a woman is in labor.) Letting the warm water hold my belly felt amazing.

By dinner the "period cramps" made me pause now and then, but I was still laughing at my husband's jokes. I breathed through each wave the way I'd practiced for four months and told him, "We'll probably have a baby tomorrow."

My second baby had other plans. By 8:30 my midwife Sarah was with us, pressing my hips exactly where I needed it, while my hypnobirthing tracks played. When a moment of fear came ("I'm not a marathon runner!"), my husband said, "You totally are. You trained for this." That was all I needed. My body was made for this. I just had to let it.

I stood up, held on to the headboard, and let my body push. The ring of fire is real, but it lasted seconds. Then, swoosh, my second baby arrived, eyes wide open, looking around the room. So awake. So beautiful.

She nursed in my arms for 45 minutes. I felt tired, hungry and so, so happy. There was intensity, yes, but I never felt like I was suffering, because every wave brought her closer to me. I felt in complete power the entire time.

That's the birth story I'll be telling for the rest of my life.

What I'd tell my first-time self

If something feels off, even if you can't put it into words yet, pause. Write it down. Ask questions. There's almost always another way. We live in a modern world with ancient instincts, so listen to yours. ❤️

I'm sharing this not to say a hospital is wrong. For some women and some pregnancies, it's exactly the right place, and I'm grateful it exists. I'm sharing it because no one told me I had another option until my second pregnancy. I want you to know sooner.

More stories are coming. In the weekly Born in the Nest letter, I'll share calm, real stories from other mothers: home births, birth center births, and births where plans changed and still felt good. Always gentle, never scary.

Have a story to share? If you've given birth at home or in a birth center and would like to help another mom feel braver, just write to me at hello@borninthenest.com. I'll always ask your permission before sharing anything, and I can keep your name private.

With love,Sybille 🤍

Know someone who's expecting? Send her this. 💛

## My midwives saw what I needed before I said a word
URL: https://borninthenest.com/lessons/day-4.html
Free lesson 4 of 5 from Born in the Nest: How midwives watch over you, and how to find comfort without an epidural.

Free lesson 4 of 5 · Home birth, explained by a mom who's done it
🌬️My midwives saw what I needed before I said a word
How midwives watch over you, and how to find comfort without an epidural.

My midwives felt a little like superheroes to me. They paid attention to everything: what I was eating, how I was sleeping, how I was really feeling, and the small things I'd never have thought to mention. Often they seemed to understand what I needed just by looking at me, before I said a word. That quiet attention was the most powerful thing I experienced, and it's a big part of how midwives care for you.

When I asked my midwives whether I needed a doula, they smiled and said, "We are your doula." They were with me the whole way, not coming and going on shifts.

Because the question every mom asks is "But what if something goes wrong?" And it's a good one. Feeling calm isn't only about candles and quiet. It's also about knowing someone skilled is watching, and that there's a plan.

How midwives keep watch

Your midwife listens to your baby's heartbeat regularly throughout labor, checks your blood pressure, pulse, and temperature, and watches how labor is progressing. She's trained to notice early signs that something needs more help, often long before it becomes urgent.

When a home birth might still be possible.

Ask before you rule it out. That's my biggest wish for you here.

In my first pregnancy, I was told at the hospital that I had high blood pressure. It turned out to be nerves: hospitals just made me nervous. That's simply my story, not medical advice, but it taught me to ask questions before deciding what was possible for me.

So don't rule yourself out too fast. A breech baby or twins don't automatically take a home or birth-center birth off the table to talk about. Some experienced midwives can talk through your options with you, like trying to turn a breech baby before labor, which is called external cephalic version. I knew women at my birth center who had twins. To be honest with you, ACOG, the organization of US obstetricians, advises against planned home birth with twins, a baby who isn't head-down, or after a previous cesarean. So the message isn't "it's fine." It's "ask an experienced midwife or doctor about your options."

And some things really do change the plan. With conditions like diabetes that needs medication or preeclampsia, guidelines suggest giving birth where obstetric care is right there. The right person to help you decide is an experienced midwife or doctor who knows you.

What a transfer usually looks like

In a large US study of almost 17,000 planned home births, about 9 out of 10 women gave birth at home. When plans changed, it was usually because of a long, slow labor. If you do move, your midwife comes with you and shares your notes. If this is your first baby, it's worth talking through your plan early with your midwife.

Did you know? 🌿 No clock on the cord. You wait for your baby, not a schedule. Many home birth midwives wait to clamp the cord until it stops pulsing on its own. It's pretty magical to watch. Wherever you give birth, you can ask about delayed cord clamping and add it to your birth plan.

Comfort, the gentle way

Remember Day 1? Fear makes us tense, and tension makes pain feel stronger. Childbirth pioneer Grantly Dick-Read called this the fear-tension-pain cycle, and Marie Mongan built her hypnobirthing method on breaking it. Here's what helps:

Warm water. A birth pool or bath. A Cochrane review found it slightly lowered the use of epidurals.
Movement. Swaying, walking, leaning over a ball or the bed.
Calm birth breathing. Slow breaths, long on the exhale, practiced for weeks before so your body knows them.
Touch and sound. Massage, counter-pressure on your lower back, low humming, a soft, loose jaw.
Laughter and love. Ina May noticed that laughter and affection help labor flow. They really are part of the toolkit!

Today's practice: breathe in for 4, out for 6, and let your jaw go loose. Do it for two minutes tonight before sleep.

Sources Cheyney et al. 2014, MANA Statistics Project · ACOG, Planned Home Birth FAQ · Cluett et al. 2018, Cochrane · OpenStax, Hypnobirthing: The Mongan Method · ACOG, If Your Baby Is Breech · NICE NG235, Intrapartum care: planning place of birth

With love,Sybille 🤍

## The question no one asked me before my first birth
URL: https://borninthenest.com/lessons/day-5.html
Free lesson 5 of 5 from Born in the Nest: A simple comparison, the questions to ask, and what comes next.

Free lesson 5 of 5 · Home birth, explained by a mom who's done it
🌱The question no one asked me before my first birth
A simple comparison, the questions to ask, and what comes next.

Before my first birth, no one ever asked me the most important question: Where do you want to give birth? I didn't even know it was a choice.

You made it to Day 5! Here's the big idea one more time: you have a choice, and your body does its best work where you feel calm and loved.

Your three options, simply

🏡 Home birth: your own space, a midwife you know, and the people you love around you. It's planned for healthy, low-risk pregnancies, with a qualified midwife and a clear transfer plan, and it usually involves fewer interventions like inductions, episiotomies and cesareans. Every pregnancy is different, so talk your options through with an experienced midwife or doctor who knows you.

🌿 Birth center: a home-like, midwife-led space outside the hospital, with comfy beds and birth tubs. It's a beautiful middle path and a lovely choice for a first baby. In a large US study, about 6 in 100 women who started labor in a birth center ended up with a cesarean.

🏥 Hospital: the right place for higher-risk pregnancies, or if you know you'd like an epidural. Many hospitals have midwives on the team too, and you can bring calm with you: dim lights, your own music, and your breathing.

Your first gentle steps

Find a midwife. You'll see two main types: CNMs (certified nurse-midwives, licensed in every state) and CPMs (certified professional midwives, who specialize in out-of-hospital birth; licensing varies by state). Try the ACNM, NARM, and American Association of Birth Centers directories.
Book a free consultation with one or two. Most offer one.
Ask these questions:How many births have you attended, and what's your training?
How do you prepare women for birth?
What nutrition and lifestyle advice do you give during pregnancy?
What does labor actually feel like when I'm not numb?
Who's your backup, and who comes with you to births?
What happens if I need to transfer to a hospital, and which hospital do you use?
What equipment and medicines do you bring?
How will my partner be part of it?
What does it cost, and does my insurance cover a birth center or home birth?
Do I have to decide right now, or when?

Notice how you feel after talking with her. How do you know a midwife or birth center feels right for you? You feel calm, heard and loved, and your gut says yes.

When you're ready to read more: Ina May's Guide to Childbirth and Spiritual Midwifery by Ina May Gaskin (her famous reminder: "your body is not a lemon"), HypnoBirthing: The Mongan Method by Marie Mongan, and The Heart in the Womb by Dr. Amali Lokugamage, an obstetrician's gentle look at love and birth. Ina May's books include many detailed birth stories, so skip any that feel like too much.

Sources ACOG, Planned Home Birth FAQ · Stapleton et al. 2013, National Birth Center Study II · ACNM credential comparison (2026)

With love from my nest to yours,Sybille 🤍

Know someone who's expecting? Send her this. 💛

What if giving birth could be the most beautiful day of your life? Five free lessons on home birth & birth centers, plus a weekly letter from a mom of two.

The birth experience no one told you was possible.

What if giving birth could be the most beautiful day of your life?

Home birth, explained by a mom who's done it, and a gentle guide through your pregnancy to the most important day of your life.

Every Sunday, I'll walk beside you through your pregnancy, the way my midwives walked beside me. Read a sample letter →

In the movies, birth is a woman screaming while everyone rushes around her. We've seen that scene so many times that most of us grow up believing it's what birth is. It isn't. Your body already knows how to give birth, and it does its best work where you feel safe, calm and loved. I'm Sybille, a mom of two. My first baby was born in a hospital and my second at home, and the difference changed everything for me.

Five free lessons · no signup needed

Your options
You have more choices than you think.

Most of us grow up picturing just one way to have a baby. Many women never hear that, alongside a hospital, they can also choose a birth center or a home birth with a midwife. Born in the Nest gently opens that door, so you can see every option and choose what feels right for you. No pressure, no lectures, just possibilities (and maybe a snack).

Your birth options, explained →
Get the weekly letter

Home birth, honestly

A few myths, gently untangled.

MythHome birth is only for very, very crunchy people.
FactIt's a recognized choice. ACOG, the organization of US obstetricians, says you have the right to choose where you give birth, and more than 58,000 US babies were born at home in 2024 (CDC final birth data).

MythAt home, you're on your own if plans change.
FactA planned home birth is made with a qualified midwife and a hospital transfer plan arranged before labor, as ACOG recommends. In a US study of 16,924 planned home births, about 9 in 10 moms gave birth at home, and most moves to the hospital were for a long, slow labor.

MythWithout a hospital, there's nothing for the pain.
FactMany midwives bring a birth pool, and a Cochrane review found that laboring in warm water slightly reduced the use of epidurals. Some moms want stronger relief than home can offer, and that's okay too.

Why so many moms love it

Your own nest. Your bed, your people, your snacks, your playlist.

Fewer interventions. ACOG notes that planned home births usually involve fewer inductions, episiotomies and cesareans.

A midwife who knows you. In a Cochrane review, women with midwife-led continuity of care were more likely to have a spontaneous vaginal birth and less likely to have an epidural.

Home birth is planned for healthy, low-risk pregnancies, and it isn't right for every pregnancy. ACOG recommends against it with twins, a baby who isn't head-down, or after a previous cesarean. But ask before you rule it out: an experienced midwife or doctor who knows you can help you find what fits. When a home birth might still be possible →

Born in the Nest
The birth story you'll want to tell.

With my first baby, I had an epidural in the hospital. I was completely numb, and I felt helpless. I had no idea what labor really feels like. I just assumed it was supposed to be scary and a little insane.

With my second child, at home, it was different. I got a real break between every contraction, so it felt doable and manageable, and I felt very in control. My midwife always told me to get comfortable with the contractions on my own first, and call after that. It felt so manageable that I didn't think I was in real labor yet, so I told my husband not to call the midwife.

Then the pushing sensation started, and it got really serious. I hadn't even realized I'd reached that stage. That's when I knew I needed them there. Even then, I still got a break between contractions, so it stayed doable. My midwives arrived just in time, about 20 minutes before my second child was born. Until then, I'd done it all myself.

And then she was here, so fast. Pure joy. 🪺

Mom of two · Chief Nest Officer
Hi, I'm Sybille

My midwife, Sarah, and her team are some of the most amazing women in my life, and Sarah always said pregnant women need to feel loved.

I called five birth centers, and Sarah's had the plainest photos online, but the moment she picked up the phone, I felt so loved I wanted to tell her everything.

That's the feeling I want you to have, every week of your pregnancy.

## About Sybille · Born in the Nest
URL: https://borninthenest.com/about.html
Hi, I'm Sybille, a mom of two. My first baby was born in a hospital and my second at home. Why I created Born in the Nest.

About
Hi, I'm Sybille

My mission: that every woman knows she has a choice in where and how she gives birth, and feels calm, loved and prepared, whatever she chooses.

I'm a mom of two. My first baby was born in a hospital with an epidural. I was completely numb, and I felt helpless. My second was born at home with a midwife I trusted, and that birth showed me how calm and beautiful giving birth can be. Same body, completely different birth. The biggest difference was where I was and how calm and loved I felt.

As my midwife Sarah always said, pregnant women need to feel loved.

That's what Born in the Nest is about.

My midwives felt a little like superheroes to me. They paid attention to everything: what I was eating, how I was sleeping, how I was really feeling, and the small things I'd never have thought to mention. Often they seemed to understand what I needed just by looking at me, before I said a word.

Why Born in the Nest exists

No one told me I had another option until my second pregnancy. I want you to know sooner.

Many women think home birth is only for the craziest people. I'd love to gently change that. 😄

Choosing where to give birth, and finding the right midwife or birth center, are big decisions, and I wish I'd had someone I could count on when I made them. When I was pregnant, just a message from one of my midwives could calm me down and make my whole day feel lighter. That's what I want Born in the Nest to be for you: a warm, trusted place you can come back to whenever you need it.

It isn't a one-time thing. The five short lessons are free right here on the site, for anyone, no signup needed. And if you'd like, I'll send you a weekly letter every Sunday, matched to your due month, the way a loving midwife would walk beside you. You're never alone on this journey. Think of it as a steady hand with you every week, all the way to the day you meet your baby.

With love from my nest to yours,Sybille 🤍

## A sample weekly letter (weeks 20–24) · Born in the Nest
URL: https://borninthenest.com/sample-letter.html
A sample of the free Born in the Nest weekly letter for weeks 20–24 of pregnancy: what's happening now, what to focus on and questions for your care team.

A sample of the weekly letter
💌Halfway there 🌸
What a weekly letter looks like, written for around weeks 20–24.

A sample letter. Every Sunday's letter is matched to where you are in your pregnancy, and this one is written for around weeks 20–24.

SubjectHalfway there 🌸 (and a word about marathons)

Hi there,

You're around weeks 20–24 now. Halfway! 🌸 In case no one has told you yet this week: you're doing beautifully.

🏡 One honest moment

When my second child was being born, a moment of fear showed up, and I blurted out, "I'm not a marathon runner!"

My husband said, "You totally are. You trained for this."

He was right, in the gentlest way. I've never run a marathon. But for about four months before my second child was born, I practiced breathing through each wave. Small, quiet practice, again and again, until my body knew it by heart. When the big day came, it was there for me.

So this letter is about training. The soft kind. No running shoes required.

🌱 What's happening around now

Little flutters. Many women start to feel their baby move somewhere around now: tiny bubbles, taps or flutters. With a first baby it often comes a little later, and every pregnancy has its own timing.
The anatomy scan. Many women are offered a detailed ultrasound, often called the anatomy scan, somewhere around weeks 18–22. It can feel exciting and a little nerve-racking at the same time. Both are okay.
A bit more energy. Many women find this middle stretch of pregnancy brings some energy back. If that's you, enjoy it. If it isn't, rest is part of the training too.

💛 What to focus on this week

Two minutes of breathing. Tonight before sleep, breathe in for 4 and out for 6, and let your jaw go loose. That's it. You're not doing it for tonight. You're doing it for the day you meet your baby.
Fuel and move in a way you enjoy. The day my second child was born looked completely ordinary: coffee, my weekly 45-minute walk, lunch, my daily stretches. (And a steak dinner. About five minutes later it was go time. Zero regrets. 🥩) Ask your midwife or doctor what movement and food look like for your pregnancy, then find a version that feels good.

🩺 Questions worth asking your midwife or doctor

What will you look at during my anatomy scan, and what happens next if anything needs a closer look?
What kind of movement and exercise feels right for my pregnancy right now?
What does good fuel look like for me these days, and is there anything you'd like me to keep an eye on?
When should I start practicing breathing or relaxation for birth, and are there classes you'd recommend?

My midwives paid attention to everything: what I was eating, how I was sleeping, how I was really feeling. So bring all of it to your next visit. And the advice I'd give my first-time self: if something feels off, even if you can't put it into words yet, pause. Write it down. Ask questions.

💌 Coming next week

Your birth preferences: what matters most to you, and a calm "if plans change" page.

Until then, hit reply and tell me: have you felt those first little flutters yet? I read every message.

With love from my nest to yours,Sybille 🤍Mom of two · Chief Nest Officer, Born in the Nest

Education only, not medical advice. Always talk with your licensed midwife or doctor about your own pregnancy.

## Privacy · Born in the Nest
URL: https://borninthenest.com/privacy.html
How Born in the Nest handles your information, in plain English: what we collect (just your email, due month and first name), why, and how to unsubscribe.

Privacy
Your privacy, in plain English
Short, honest, and no fine-print surprises.

Last updated: October 23, 2026

Who we are

Born in the Nest is a small, gentle guide to birth choices, run by HyperLaunch LLC, a Utah company. If you ever have a question about your privacy, write to me at hello@borninthenest.com. I read every message.

What we collect

Only what you give us when you sign up: your email address, your due month and, if you'd like, your first name. That's it.

Why we collect it

To send you what you asked for: the weekly letter, every Sunday of your pregnancy, matched to your due month. Your due month is how we match each letter to where you are. If you share your first name, we use it to say hello properly. The five lessons are free on the site, so you don't need to share anything to read them.

We never sell or share your information

Not with advertisers, not with anyone. Your details are used only to send you Born in the Nest emails.

The services we use

Kit (formerly ConvertKit) sends our emails and keeps your email address, due month and first name secure for us. Like most email services, Kit can tell us whether an email was opened or a link was clicked, which helps us write emails that are actually useful. Kit doesn't sell your information. You can read Kit's privacy policy and how Kit handles subscriber data.

GitHub Pages hosts this website. Like any web host, GitHub may keep basic technical logs (such as IP addresses) to keep the site secure and running. Here's GitHub's privacy statement.

No tracking cookies

This website doesn't use analytics, advertising or tracking cookies. Even our fonts are hosted on our own site, so your visit isn't shared with font services. If that ever changes, we'll update this page first.

Unsubscribe anytime

Every email has an unsubscribe link at the bottom. One click and you're off the list, no hard feelings. You can also write to us anytime to ask what we have about you, to correct it, or to delete it, and we'll take care of it.

Education only

Born in the Nest shares education only. It isn't medical advice and doesn't replace care from your licensed midwife or doctor. Please talk to your provider about anything health-related. In an emergency, call 911.

If this page changes

We'll update the date at the top of this page.

With love from my nest to yours,Sybille 🤍
